claims.text: Moderate aluminum addition in near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni promotes short-range chemical ordering.
Short-range chemical ordering generates local lattice distortions.
Moderate aluminum-induced ordering increases stacking-fault energy.
Ordering-induced lattice distortions raise the energy barrier for phase transformations.
The proposed changes suppress the formation of deleterious secondary phases.
Moderate aluminum-induced ordering stabilizes a single-phase FCC structure over a wide range of temperatures and stress conditions.
A stable single-phase FCC microstructure is necessary for retaining a balanced combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
A near-equiatomic, single-phase FCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy can serve as the initial material state after standard processing.
Samples with moderate aluminum-induced ordering will have improved high-temperature strength relative to the baseline.
Samples with moderate aluminum-induced ordering will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced defects than the baseline.
Samples with moderate aluminum-induced ordering will have better corrosion or environmental resistance than the baseline.
Samples with moderate aluminum-induced ordering will have enhanced cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions when processing avoids large-scale compositional segregation.
Extreme deviations in aluminum content or addition of other major alloying elements may fall outside the proposed mechanism.
Aluminum content or processing treatment can be systematically varied to modulate short-range order.
An increase in short-range order should correlate with improved phase stability and retention of the targeted properties.
The optimal aluminum concentration has not been quantitatively determined.
The quantitative relationship between short-range order and property improvement remains undetermined.
